articles.text: Pending school board approval during the August 12 meeting, the board has selected Donald Evans as Piedmont Unified School District’s interim superintendent for the year. Dr. Evans came out of retirement to be Piedmont’s interim superintendent during the 2022-23 school year, after Randy Booker’s departure and before Jennifer Hawn. “[Evans] has a tremendous amount of experience, serving as the superintendent of Berkeley Unified School District for six years before retiring in 2019, and as the superintendent of Hayward Unified School District before that,” the board said in an August 9 press release. Since Evans last served as the leader of Piedmont schools in 2023, he has stayed busy in retirement. He was the interim superintendent in 2024 in Albany and has worked with the California Collaborative for Educational Excellence. Evans also provides executive coaching for district leaders in the Bay Area and has been a lecturer at California State University, East Bay since 2022. Dr. Evans’ career in education began in the classroom as an elementary school teacher before finding his niche in administration as a vice principal and then a principal. He received his bachelor’s degree from University of Delaware, his master’s from United States International University, and earned his Doctorate of Education from the University of California, Berkeley. ”We are thrilled to welcome him back to the district, where he has well-established relationships with our administrators and staff,” stated the board. With Evans’ arrival, the district won’t skip a beat following Hawn’s departure for Cupertino. Evans joined Hawn on the Piedmont campus for the first day of school on Monday, where he was greeted by parents happy to see his familiar face. Donald Evans (left), pictured with School Board President Ruchi Medhekar and outgoing superintendent Jennifer Hawn, will be Piedmont Unified School District’s interim superintendent for the second time.

Even the demographics that traditionally read the most – retirees, women, and college graduates – Horowitch also points out that “Americans get much less of their news through reading than they once did. In 1975, about half of 20-somethings said that they read the newspaper every day. Today, less than 10 percent do … and 40 percent say they prefer to watch or listen to online news rather But let’s pause for a moment and examine what Horowitch means when she refers to this change as a “literacy crisis,” or “the end of reading.” Her choice of words is not intended to be hyperbolic; rather she is drawing our attention to a profound social transformation, not dissimilar from that which occurred post-Gutenberg. She refers to this moment not as one in which we cannot decode individual words. In fact, she suggests, “Americans are reading more words than ever before. What has changed is what they read and how.” And therein, as the Bard long ago stated, “is the rub.” I recall an image from a period film, set during the Great Depression, which showed a silent room full of seated, unemployed men looking for work, each reading a newspaper. It was the worst of times for many, made manifest in that room of white sails. But that was then, and this is now. Clearly those waiting today for an appointment, an interview perhaps, or for a subway (or seated on a subway), or even at a dinner table are looking intently down at a small screen. Each, as Horowitch describes, is “bombarded with emails, text messages, X posts, Reddit threads, Instagram captions.” She refers to this beckoning cascade of messages as an “explosion of textual fragments” that compete with devoting our attention to longer written works that convey rich and complicated information. Horowitch goes on to cite Maryanne Wolf, a cognitive neuroscientist at UCLA, who states that “people are losing the ability to think deeply about writing. That doesn’t mean they are forgetting how to decode individual words. Rather, they are losing the higher-order abilities of comprehension and synthesis. America, in other words, isn’t illiterate. articles.text: Since 2023, Piedmont’s home electrification rebates have supported 90 gas-to-electric appliance conversions and electrical panel updates. Over the same period, home electrification has gained ground locally. In 2025, permits for heat pump and heat pump water heater installations surpassed their natural gas equivalents for the first time. But natural gas use in Piedmont homes still accounts for around half of community-wide greenhouse gas emissions, and continued progress is needed to meet the city’s climate goals. Updates to the rebate program take what the city has learned from the first three years and put it to work by expanding the projects the city supports, improving access to higher rebates, and focusing city funds where they can have the greatest impact. Projects eligible for rebates now include solar paired with battery storage, standalone battery storage, gas meter removal, and smart electrical panels: • Heat pump water heater: $800 standard rebate; up to $2,000 for income-qualified • Solar + battery system: $2,000 standard rebate; up to $5,000 for income-qualified • Electrical panel improvements: $900 standard rebate; up to $2,250 for income-qualified • Gas meter removal: $2,500 for all eligible households Under the new eligibility rules, heat pump heating and cooling rebates are limited to incomequalified households. City data showed that these projects were moving forward without a rebate, while rebates appeared to play a greater role in heat pump water heater projects. Redirecting those funds allows the program to support more projects and better target assistance where it can make a difference. Sustainability Award honoree Jeff Fucigna with his heat pump water heater Sustainability Award honoree Brandon Bercovich with upgraded electrical panels For residents who already submitted a permit application for a heat pump project that would have qualified under the previous rules, the city is providing a grace period and accepting applications for the standard rebate until October 1. The city has expanded eligibility for higher, “income-qualified,” rebate amounts. Previously, income-qualified rebates were tied to CARE or FERA eligibility, which applies to only about 2% of Piedmont households. In three years, just one rebate was issued at the income-qualified level. Analysis found that these limits were not reaching many households that may still face financial barriers to electrification. Now, households earning up to 120% of Area Median Income (roughly $195,000/year for a 4-person household) can qualify for a new “moderate-income” rebate tier. Households that qualify for CARE or FERA will continue to receive the highest rebate amounts. Before starting a project, review current rebate amounts and eligibility requirements at piedmont.ca.gov/Electrification-Rebates. Rebates are firstcome, first-served, and funding is not guaranteed.

articles.text: I’ve been thinking a lot lately about connection as a muscle. For most of human history, and honestly for most of our own lives, until pretty recently, we got a lot of tiny social “reps” without trying very hard. When we walked into a store, we talked to the cashier. If we got lost, we asked someone for directions. We chatted with the person next to us in line or made small talk with the barista while waiting for our regular coffee order. We walked through the world without earbuds in our ears and a phone in our hand. And while none of these interactions felt especially meaningful because they honestly weren’t, they served a very important purpose. They were moments of connection reps. Tiny moments of eye contact, noticing another person, saying something, responding, adjusting, laughing, recovering from awkwardness. And all those reps added up. Today, a lot of those moments have quietly disappeared. We order through apps and use self-checkout. We text instead of call. We put in earbuds and fill every pause by looking at a screen. Again, none of these things are bad. They are convenient and I use all of them, but I do wonder what happens when we stop doing the little lifts. Because then, when we need to do the big connection lifts, they somehow feel much harder. Things like starting a conversation with someone new or inviting a potential friend to coffee. Or walking into a room where you don’t know anyone and then asking a question that might feel vulnerable. These are all heavier connection lifts. And if our connection muscles have been slowly atrophying, it makes sense that they would feel harder than they used to. So maybe, the answer is not to start with the biggest, bravest version of connection. Maybe we need to start doing little reps again. This month’s experiment is simple: look for one tiny social interaction each day that you would normally skip. For instance, say something to the cashier instead of looking at your phone and remember to ask the barista how their day is going. Try to take out your earbuds on a walk and choose to make one phone call instead of sending a text. The goal is not to become wildly extroverted or strike up deep conversations with strangers; it’s to simply exercise the connection muscle. Connection is not only built in the big moments, it is built in hundreds of tiny acts of social courage and attention that teach us, over and over again, how to be with other people. For most of human history, and honestly for most of our own lives, until pretty recently, we got a lot of tiny social “reps” without trying very hard. When we walked into a store, we talked to the cashier. If we got lost, we asked someone for directions. We chatted with the person next to us in line or made small talk with the barista while waiting for our regular coffee order. We walked through the world without earbuds in our ears and a phone in our hand. And while none of these interactions felt especially meaningful because they honestly weren’t, they served a very important purpose. They were moments of connection reps. Tiny moments of eye contact, noticing another person, saying something, responding, adjusting, laughing, recovering from awkwardness. And all those reps added up. Today, a lot of those moments have quietly disappeared. We order through apps and use self-checkout. We text instead of call. We put in earbuds and fill every pause by looking at a screen. Again, none of these things are bad. They are convenient and I use all of them, but I do wonder what happens when we stop doing the little lifts. Because then, when we need to do the big connection lifts, they somehow feel much harder. Things like starting a conversation with someone new or inviting a potential friend to coffee. Or walking into a room where you don’t know anyone and then asking a question that might feel vulnerable. These are all heavier connection lifts. And if our connection muscles have been slowly atrophying, it makes sense that they would feel harder than they used to. So maybe, the answer is not to start with the biggest, bravest version of connection. Maybe we need to start doing little reps again. This month’s experiment is simple: look for one tiny social interaction each day that you would normally skip. For instance, say something to the cashier instead of looking at your phone and remember to ask the barista how their day is going. Try to take out your earbuds on a walk and choose to make one phone call instead of sending a text. The goal is not to become wildly extroverted or strike up deep conversations with strangers; it’s to simply exercise the connection muscle. Connection is not only built in the big moments, it is built in hundreds of tiny acts of social courage and attention that teach us, over and over again, how to be with other people. And the good news about muscles is that even when they get a little weak, they can get stronger again. We just have to notice and then start doing the reps again. articles.text: LUCAS SMOLKO Tennis Piedmont High Class of 2026 UC Santa Cruz Class of 2030 We recently named Lucas Smolko our 2026 Athlete of the Year after finishing his Piedmont High career in illustrious fashion. He won the school’s first North Coast Section Individual Tournament singles title since Barry Gilbert in 1975 by claiming the D2 crown on May 9, and won his third consecutive Western Alameda County Conference singles title on May 1. He is the only repeat and three-time singles champion in the league tournament on the boys’ side. For the NCS title, Smolko defeated Acalanes’ Sze Ting Chen in straight sets 6-4, 6-3. To get there, he shutout St. Patrick’s Oscar Swenson 6-0, 6-0 in the opening round, won 6-1, 6-4 win over Armaan Mishra of Lick-Wilmerding in the quarterfinals, and shut down Stuart Hall’s Edward Morfit 6-1, 6-0 in the semifinals. His win over Chen was a rematch of Piedmont’s February 26’s match against Acalanes, where Smolko lost 6-3, 7-6. For the WACC singles crown, he defeated Castro Valley’s Guhan Anandkumar in straight sets by scores of 6-2, 6-3 as the top seeded player. He was our honorable menLucas Smolko recently graduated from Piedmont High and embarks on his freshman year on UC Santa Cruz’s tennis team. tion for 2024 Sophomore of the Year, and our 2023 Freshman of the Year. Piedmont High named Smolko the school’s boys’ Oustanding Senior Athlete in 2026. Lucas will continue his tennis career at UC Santa Cruz. What is your workout program this summer? My workout program has been cultivated by my UC Santa Cruz tennis coach. I am expecting to do specific strength training exercises multiple times a week and do 5k runs weekly. This conditioning has been easing me into all the training I will be doing with the tennis team. What are your fitness goals for the summer? My summer fitness goal is to prepare myself as much as possible for my tennis season. By the time I start college I want to be able to run a 5k in under 21 minutes as that will be weekly conditioning with the team. How are you measuring your development? When I am working on my cardio I go to the Piedmont track and time most of my runs to track progress. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I work with a private trainer once a week on strength training and lift weights at home as well. When working out I have been incorporating new workouts from the UCSC tennis coach that I will be using with my team. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? A recent milestone I accomplished was reaching clay court nationals in Florida. It was very difficult to gain enough points to be accepted into the tournament. In addition to traveling and playing many tournaments I trained a lot in the weeks leading up to the event to prepare myself for playing on clay along with very hot and humid conditions. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? I would advise younger athletes to set achievable goals in your sport and plan out how you can reach them. articles.text: “Big Picnic” closes out festival’s 89th season Public Enemy Stern Grove Festival will conclude its 89th season next weekend with its annual Big Picnic Weekend, featuring performances by hip-hop group Public Enemy on Saturday, August 15, and soul singer Al Green on Sunday, August 16. The concerts will take place at Sigmund Stern Grove, a natural amphitheater surrounded by eucalyptus, redwood and fir trees at 19th Avenue and Sloat Boulevard in San Francisco. Founded in 1938, Stern Grove Festival is the West Coast’s longest-running free outdoor music festival. The summer concert series has presented more than eight decades of performances spanning music, opera, theater and dance. The Big Picnic Weekend serves as the festival’s annual fundraiser. While general admission to Stern Grove Festival performances is free, picnic table seating for the final weekend is available for purchase, with proceeds supporting the festival and helping keep its concert series free for more than 110,000 people who attend the festival each summer. Public Enemy will headline Saturday’s concert. Formed in Long Island, New York, in 1985 and led by Chuck D and Flavor Flav, Public Enemy was inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2013 and is known for albums including “It Takes a Nation of Millions to Hold Us Back” and “Fear of a Black Planet.” Sunday’s lineup will be led by Al Green, the Grammy-winning soul singer best known for hits including “Let’s Stay Together,” “Tired of Being Alone” and “Take Me to the River.” Green, whose career began in the 1960s, was inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 1995. His performance will also feature Oakland singer Goapele and The Glide Ensemble, the gospel choir associated with San Francisco’s Glide Memorial Church. Doors open at noon both days, with performances beginning at 2 p.m. Picnic table seating remains available for the Big Picnic Weekend. Table purchases are considered donations to Stern Grove Festival and are nonrefundable. Visit https://www.sterngrove. org/big-picnic to purchase picnic table tickets. articles.text: San Francisco Ballet School students will perform at the Flower Piano festival at the San Francisco Botanical Garden in September as part of the annual outdoor music event. The festival is scheduled for September 10 through 20 at the 55-acre garden and will feature 12 grand and baby grand pianos placed throughout the grounds. Visitors can attend scheduled performances, watch community groups perform and play the pianos themselves during designated open-play sessions. The San Francisco Ballet School is among the performers scheduled for this year’s festival. The school’s performances will give audiences an opportunity to see ballet students perform in an outdoor setting as part of a festival that combines music and community programming. Flower Piano was established in 2015 by Sunset Piano founders Mauro Ffortissimo and Dean Mermell in partnership with the Gardens of Golden Gate Park. The event has since become an annual festival at the botanical garden. Other performers scheduled for the 2026 festival include La Gente SF, Sixth Station Trio, Tango No. 9 and the Kev Choice Chamber Ensemble. The ensemble’s repertoire combines hiphop, jazz and classical music. The festival also will feature an expanded Flower Piano Lounge in the Celebration Garden, with seating, food and beverages, along with evening performances. During open-play periods, the pianos will be available for visitors of all ages and skill levels. Organizers recommend that attendees bring picnic blankets because seating is not guaranteed. Additional infor mation, including the performance schedule and ticket information, is available through the Gardens of Golden Gate Park at https://gggp. org/flowerpiano/. The San Francisco Ballet School is among the performers scheduled for this year’s festival.

articles.text: San Francisco Opera and San Francisco Opera Guild will open the company’s 104th season with its annual fundraising gala “Opera Ball” on September 12. The evening will begin with a cocktail reception and dinner at San Francisco City Hall before the opening night performance of Giuseppe Verdi’s Simon Boccanegra at the War Memorial Opera House. An after-party at City Hall will follow the performance. Proceeds from the event will benefit San Francisco Opera and San Francisco Opera Guild’s artistic and K-12 education programs. This year’s Opera Ball is dedicated to Diane B. Wilsey in recognition of her 20 years as Opening Weekend Grand Sponsor, supporting Opera Ball, the season-opening performance and Opera in the Park. “Opera Ball is more than the opening night of the opera season, it is one of the Bay Area’s defining fall galas,” co-chairs Sydney Leung and Jennifer Walske said in a joint statement. “Most importantly, every ticket supports our house of creativity, San Francisco Opera, and brings the transformative power of music education to K–12 students throughout the Bay Area through San Francisco Opera Guild.” Music Director Eun Sun Kim will conduct the San Francisco Opera Orchestra and Chorus in Verdi’s political drama, which is set in 14th-century Genoa. The cast includes Mongolian baritone Amartuvshin Enkhbat in the title role, soprano Eleonora Buratto as Amelia and Maria, tenor Joshua Guerrero as Gabriele Adorno, and bass-baritone Christian Van Horn as Jacopo Fiesco. The production is directed by Katherine M. Carter in Claus Guth’s staging from Hamburg State Opera. For tickets, visit sfopera.com, call (415) 864-3330 or visit the Box Office in the lobby of the War Memorial Opera House at 301 Van Ness Avenue. San Francisco Opera’s annual fundraiser benefits education programs in San Francisco.

articles.text: San Francisco Playhouse concludes its 2025-26 season with the Tony Award-winning musical Hairspray, running now through September 12. Set in 1962 Baltimore, Hairspray follows teenager Tracy Turnblad as she pursues a spot on the popular television program “The Corny Collins Show.” After achieving her dream, Tracy uses her newfound platform to challenge racial segregation and advocate for integration. The musical features a score by Marc Shaiman and Scott Wittman, including songs such as “You Can’t Stop the Beat,” “Good Morning Baltimore,” “Welcome to the ‘60s” and “I Know Where I’ve Been.” The book is by Mark O’Donnell and Thomas Meehan. San Francisco Playhouse Artistic Director Bill English directs the production, with Phaedra Tillery-Boughton serving as associate director, Dave Dobrusky as musical director and Phoenyx Rose as choreographer. “In San Francisco Playhouse’s new production, we will reimagine Hairspray with a sharper edge, stripping away some of its bubblegum sheen to restore the subversive bite of John Waters,” English said in a press release. “This production leans into the story’s racial politics and cultural satire, examining Baltimore’s fight for integration through our contemporary lens.” Based on the 1988 film by John Waters, Hairspray premiered at Seattle’s 5th Avenue Theatre before opening on Broadway, where it won eight Tony Awards, including Best Musical, and ran for more than eight years. The musical later opened in London’s West End, winning four Olivier Awards, and has since been adapted into a feature film and a live television production. Director Bill English said the production “becomes more than a feel-good musical… in an era marked by polarization, erasure, and the lingering shadows of racist ideology.” “It’s a defiant, joyful call to resistance, where dancing is protest and inclusion is revolutionary,” he added. Ella Ruth Francis will make her San Francisco Playhouse debut as Tracy Turnblad. Trevor March returns to the company as Link Larkin after appearing in “Into the Woods.” Jeffrey Brian Adams will play Corny Collins, while Samantha Rich portrays Penny Pingleton and Jordan Covington returns as Seaweed J. Stubbs. Jonathan Chisolm makes their Playhouse debut as Edna Turnblad alongside Ken Brill as Wilbur Turnblad. Mackenzie Macdonald will portray Amber Von Tussle, with Alison Ewing as Velma Von Tussle and Jeannine Anderson as Motormouth Maybelle. The cast also includes Rebecca Pingree as Prudy Pingleton, David Boyll as Mr. Pinky and Harriman F. Spritzer, Sanaiya Johnson and Suleika Onia Patton alternating as Little Inez, Kareem Jenkins as Duane, Kaila Dyson, Anese Jade and Cai Rodis as The Dynamites, and Sierra Bolar, Matt Letton, Gwen Tessman and Hunter Yocom as The Nicest Kids in Town. Visit https://sfplayhouse. org/2025-2026-season/hairspray/ or call the box office at 415-677- 9596 to purchase tickets. Cast of San Francisco Playhouse production of Hairspray

articles.text: American Conservatory Theater’s (A.C.T.) Twelfth Night leaves the stage this Sunday, August 16. Twelfth Night was named one of the best theatrical productions of 2018 by Time Magazine, The Hollywood Reporter and The Washington Post. The play is a contemporary musical adaptation of William Shakespeare’s classic romantic comedy about mistaken identity and eventual self-discovery. Viola washes up on the shores of Illyria on the twelfth day of Christmas disguised as a man who eventually falls for a duke. Viola navigates the gender confusion in her role while she finds her true love in the process. The production and interpretation of the Shakespeare classic features an original jazz-funk score by Shaina Taub. The cast includes Nathan Bennett-Crump, Briana Bothello, Khalil Carim, Lucas Ceja, Laura Ferreira, Benjamin Grant, Mia Hangai, Ella Kim, Lourdes Verde Lombardo, Zoe Mastropasqua, Justina Mateescu and Keenan Moran. The play is directed by Dee Dee Stephens and choreographed by Meredith Joelle Charlson, with music direction by Amanda Dee. Twelfth Night is showing onstage at the Strand Theater in San Francisco now through August 16. Visit https://www. act-sf.org/whats-on/conservatory-shows/twelfth-night to purchase tickets.

articles.text: A scene from Arrested Development Are you a fan of HBO’s Succession? Do you enjoy eccentric family dynamics where no one wins? Arrested Development should be the next show on your watchlist. As its narrator (Ron Howard) states at the top of every episode: “Now the story of a wealthy family who lost everything, and the one son who had no choice but to keep them all together. It’s Arrested Development.” Most sitcoms about families settle for warmth and comfort. Arrested Development, created by Mitchell Hurwitz, has almost none of the nostalgic familial dynamic, and that’s the point. The show follows the Bluths, a once-untouchably-wealthy Orange County family who ran the Bluth Company, a successful real estate development firm, until patriarch George Bluth Sr. (Jeffrey Tambor) is arrested for fraud and embezzlement. What’s left behind is his son Michael (Jason Bateman), the only Bluth who’s ever done an honest day’s work and is so dedicated to his father’s company that he and his son George Michael (Michael Cera) live in the attic of a model home unit. But he suddenly finds himself the last responsible adult in a family that’s never once considered being responsible. Michael’s attempts to keep the Bluth Company afloat quickly become secondary to the much larger problem of keeping his family from completely falling apart. His mother Lucille (Jessica Walter) is a martini-soaked social climber who cares more about preserving her lifestyle than dealing with the family’s imminent financial collapse. His sister Lindsay (Portia de Rossi) is a shopaholic with no job experience, married to Tobias Fünke (David Cross), a former licensed psychiatrist and psychoanalyst who lost his license after performing CPR on a man who didn’t need it and has since become obsessed with pursuing an acting career he is utterly unsuited for. Their daughter Maeby (Alia Shawkat) is a scheming teenager who constantly looks for new ways to get her parents’ attention, while Michael’s brothers are hardly any easier to manage. Gob (Will Arnett) is a magician whose ego far exceeds his talent, perpetually trying to prove himself to a family that rarely takes him seriously. And Buster (Tony Hale), meanwhile, is a socially stunted man-child whose sheltered upbringing has left him almost completely unequipped to function on his own.

Saturday, September 5, 4:30 p.m. In the Tradition Jazz & Pops Piano Trio To celebrate the Fall Equinox and Mexican Independence Day, the trio will present a full program centered around Autumn Leaves. There is a narrative (story line) that ties each tune on the program into the theme for the month. For Autumn Leaves, for example, many of the tunes, such as Autumn Leaves (1947), September in the Rain (1937), Autumn In New York (1934), have an obvious connection to the autumn theme. Other tunes such as I’ve Got the World on A String (1932) and Wrap Your Troubles in Dreams (1931) do not have such an obvious connection. This is more than a concert, it’s a voyage back in time to the cabarets and jazz clubs of SaintGermain-des-Prés, where stories of love, loss, and life were sung with passion. With SonoMusette, every performance invites you to feel the pulse of Parisian life and to fall in love with these unforgettable songs all over again. While at first unsure of her eyes Bea decides to employ herself as a talent agent for notbelieved-in-anymore creations of children’s imaginations. Now, this reporter has a toddler who called this the “Ghost” movie and she liked the imagery of the imaginary friends. The Betty Boop bumble bee, and Steve Carell’s character Blue, an enormous and happy-go-lucky purple monster, come to life with modern day graphics processing power. There is a backstory about Bea’s family that opens the film and gets a little too much screentime. This dad and daughter film critic team barely stayed on the couch waiting for the shiny characters, the “ghosts,” to first appear on the screen. There is good intrigue and mystery to the story and this film employes a worthy use of AI graphics development. It’s a cute story about never being too old to believe and there’s good intrigue to the development of the plot which is to relocate these unemployed Imaginary Friends. Younger kids three to maybe eight are the target audience, but there were enough surprises to keep a babysitter capable of following along. This dad and daughter duo actually finished this one, although it took two sittings. Just crossing the finish line is a win, so great job IF, you did the trick. articles.text: Last Wednesday the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesday group had a very strong turnout of 55 walkers and six K-9 best friends at the Exedra for another special walk. As part of the group’s new initiative to ensure the longterm future of the activity, more walkers are leading walks. This morning Mary Carter was going to have the group check out the new student drop-off zones and parking around Havens School, and then take a look at beautiful old homes built before the 1906 San Francisco Earthquake. Mary led the group across Highland Avenue, past the commercial center, and up the street to a spot across from Havens’ Ellen Driscoll Playhouse, where she pointed out the new “No Parking During School Hours” signs marking the new drop-off area for Havens students. There were cars parked there this morning, but when school starts next week that will be illegal. The group crossed at the Havens crosswalk to the front entrance, another drop-off zone, and then went around the corner on Oakland Avenue to the one for preschool, TK, and kindergarten students. The walkers then went down Bonita Avenue to the middle of the block, where a gate opens into the playgrounds. This gate is on the spot where the entrance to the original Bonita Avenue School stood when it was built in 1910. The school was later renamed for Frank C. Havens, who donated the land. Much of the original building was torn down in the 1950s, replaced in 1955, and later the campus was almost entirely rebuilt. The group continued down Bonita to the historic Wetmore House, the oldest surviving house in Piedmont. Jesse L. Wetmore built it in 1878 in a New Orleans architectural style, and this wonderful house narrowly escaped being torn down. When the last Wetmore daughter died in 1939, she left the property to her maid, Myrtle Brown, but Brown died while the will was in probate, which prevented her from taking ownership. The house sat vacant until 1942, when City officials wanted to raze it for a City parking lot. Mills College art instructor Alice Putnam Erskine stepped in, purchased the home at auction through a friend for $5,200, and saved it from the wrecking ball. Erskine ultimately secured the home’s permanent survival by getting it officially listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1978. It is the only property in Piedmont with this designation. Back in the 1870s, Wetmore built a similar Southern cottage next door as a wedding gift for his daughter, Blanche, and her husband, Dr. George Sherman. The Sherman Cottage later became a Christian Science Reading Room. The City acquired the building in 2003, and in 2011 it was converted into the Piedmont Center for the Arts at 801 Magnolia. Then Mary led the walkers down Magnolia Avenue to the building that has been the home of the Piedmont Recreation Department for approximately 77 years. It was not the first building on the site. James Gamble, one of Piedmont’s first residents, bought land from Walter Blair and built a Victorian mansion on it sometime before 1883. It was Gamble who first used the Italian word “Piedmonte” to describe the hillside community that became the city of Piedmont. The name “Piedmont” remains, but Mary noted some street names have changed since then: Piedmont Avenue is now Magnolia Avenue, Vernal is Highland Avenue, and Amity is Craig Avenue. Gamble’s residence was destroyed, and a new house, owned by Ralph W. Kinney, was built on the site in 1912. The City of Piedmont bought the Kinney house in 1949 as a Recreation Center for youth, and the building’s exterior remains largely Among those participating were Dan Sedonis, Mike Henn, Jack Fischrup with K-9 best friend Kojak, Peggy Shultz, Edith Lee, June Yee, Audrey Sung, Kristin Howard, Jasmine Cai, Judy Love, Nancy Henn with K-9 best friend Roger, Stella Houston, Aileen DeSoto with K-9 best friend Hudson, Brenda Ferrero, Bonnie Sherwood with K-9 best friend Zippy, Cathy Laymon, Tyler Johnson, Deborah Curtin with K-9 best friend Brie, Mike Gallant, Diane Jimenez, Joan Jung with K-9 best friend JT, Joyce Ahern, Sherry Jacobs, Dave DeRoche, Noemi Alvarado, Pat Keller, Jim Kellogg, Ken Moy, Alissa Quan, Alicia Rivera, Bill Ahern, Melba Yee, Claire Anderson, Nancy DeRoche, Mark Davis, Rick Eigenbrode, Marcia Arthurs, Mary Carter, Pat Nicholas, Max Becker, Chuck Oraftik, Denny McGee, Jim Kuo, Albert Chen, Charlene Louie, Adrienne Hamlin, Brian Hamlin, Sanghi Wagner, Bern Shield, and Dick Carter. The Cabernet Sauvignon comes from Oakville vineyards, where the combination of warm days, cooling evening temperatures and well-drained soils is particularly well suited to producing concentrated but balanced wines. The Chardonnay, meanwhile, has long been distinguished by its Burgundian influence. In 1981, Nickel imported Grand Cru Chardonnay cuttings from Burgundy, establishing a foundation for the elegant, richly textured style associated with Far Niente. The winery itself is almost as important as the wines. Its historic stone buildings and hillside caves have been carefully preserved, creating an atmosphere that recalls Napa’s pioneering era. This year, Far Niente has also completed a sensitive renovation of its Great Hall, updating the hospitality experience while retaining the character of the historic building. Far Niente today is hardly a newcomer trying to reinvent itself. Its appeal lies in consistenly beautifully made Cabernet and Chardonnay, an extraordinary setting, and a philosophy that favors refinement over fashion. In a Napa Valley that has changed enormously over the past four decades, Far Niente remains a reminder that some of the valley’s most enduring pleasures are the simplest ones—good vineyards, careful winemaking and time. Far Niente winery is nestled among the redwoods. Outdoor tasting at Far Niente overlooks a man-made lake. Far Niente focuses on Chardonnay and Cabernet Sauvignon. • 2024 Far Niente Chardonnay The Far Niente Chardonnay has a unique sense of freshness; its aromas blooming slowly as it airs in the glass and flint, toast, beeswax give way to scents of lemon and pineapple. The palate has a silky texture and explodes with layers of concentrated tropical fruit. Its generosity is complemented by fresh acidity that adds an ethereal sensation. • 2023 Far Niente Cabernet Sauvignon Oakville The deep garnet colored Oakville Cabernet has aromas of cassis, chocolate and red currants plus underlying notes of roses, tobacco and fresh herbs. Full-bodied, the palate has a taut, muscular core of youthful, expressive black fruit framed by firm, grainy tannins and tons of freshness, finishing long and savory. • 2022 Far Niente Cabernet Sauvignon Benson Vale The Benson Vale Cabernet, the winery’s flagship, exhibits a youthful dense, purple color as well as sweet notes of graphite, oak, forest floor, black currants and leather. Crafted from a cuvee of 80% Semillon and 20% Sauvignon Blanc, the Dolce offers fragrant orange blossoms, honeycomb, and ginger scents with a core of orange marmalade, pears and spice cake. The palate is light on its feet with zippy freshness lifting the well-knit sweetness, finishing long with a skip in its step. Forgo dessert and serve this instead. Kenefick Ranch began producing its own wines in 2002. The wines are made with an emphasis on balance rather than sheer power. Native yeasts, careful vineyard work and French oak are used to produce wines with soft tannins and naturally refreshing acidity. Tom Kenefick died in 2021, but his family remains deeply involved. His son Chris is now the second-generation owner and proprietor, working alongside his wife Kali and sister Caitlin to carry on their father’s vision. articles.text: Art and music will fill every block of College Avenue when the Rockridge District Association presents Rock-N-Stroll on Saturday, August 22, from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. This free, family- and pet-friendly celebration invites visitors to spend the day exploring one of Oakland’s most beloved business districts through live music, local art, shopping, dining, and neighborhood experiences. Unlike a traditional street festival, Rock-N-Stroll keeps the streets open while encouraging visitors to wander at their own pace. Stretching from Broadway to Alcatraz Avenue, the one-mile event transforms Rockridge into an interactive celebration where every storefront, sidewalk, and gathering space offers something new to discover. More than 50 local artists, over 20 live musical performances, artisan popups, wine and food tastings, children’s activities, demonstrations, exclusive promotions, and neighborhood restaurants create an experience that celebrates the businesses and creative spirit that define Rockridge. Rather than visiting a crowded vendor village or being packed in front of a single stage, at this festival visitors are encouraged to roam throughout the district, discovering dozens of businesses offering exclusive Rock-N-Stroll experiences. Market Hall will fire up the grill for fresh sausage sandwiches and prize wheel giveaways, while Bad Walter’s Bootleg Ice Cream pairs live music with kids’ crafts. Starter Bakery celebrates with Happy Hour specials on pastries and drinks, Belly will serve taco samples throughout the afternoon, and Redfield Cider Bar & Bottle Shop features Japanese wine tastings alongside an okonomiyaki pop-up. Shopping enthusiasts will find oneday-only promotions throughout the district. Art lovers will discover even more throughout the district with pop-ups placed across a full mile. Mercy Vintage showcases Oakland-based Palestinian artist Manar Harb alongside several guest artists, and the SLATE Contemporary Gallery will host a small works exhibition and sale with artists on-site throughout the day. Preserved, The Yoni Temple, In Full Swing Plus Sizes, Saffron Kitchen, Pegasus Books and numerous other merchants will host local artists, creating an art walk that extends the entire length of College Avenue. Families can also enjoy face painting, children’s craft stations, pup-friendly stops, photo opportunities, giveaways and interactive activities around nearly every corner, making Rock-N-Stroll a destination for visitors of all ages. Rock-NStroll celebrates Oakland’s thriving creative community with an Art Bazaar featuring more than 50 local visual artists of all ages exhibiting paintings, ceramics, jewelry, prints, textiles and handcrafted works inside and outside participating businesses. Rock-N-Stroll also showcases musicians whose performances are unlike anything audiences typically encounter. The performances will feature handpan artists, jazz, blues, soul, and rock & roll, indie folk, pop, rock, electronic music, DJs, violinists, and R&B. The majority of these artists have roots in the Bay Area and are happy to perform for their community. Par ticipating merchants throughout Rockridge will offer wine and food tastings, sidewalk pop-ups, artist demonstrations, exclusive sales, craft stations, children’s activities, prize wheels, and special promotions throughout the day. The Festival Fun Zone at College Avenue Presbyterian Church serves as the community gathering place throughout the day, featuring children’s crafts, a family photo booth, raffles for Rockridge e-Gift Cards, pup water stations and treats, and information about everything happening throughout the district. If you’re looking for family activities, check the website as merchants and local artists are hosting face painters, craft stations, workshops, giveaways for kids, and more. “Rock-N-Stroll is about celebrating the people and businesses that make Rockridge such a special neighborhood,” said Jody Colley of the Rockridge District Association. “Visitors can spend the day discovering incredible musicians, meeting local artists, supporting independent businesses and enjoying great food—all while experiencing the welcoming spirit that defines our community.” Admission is free. Visitors are encouraged to take BART to Rockridge Station or enjoy available street parking while spending the day exploring College Avenue from Broadway to Alcatraz Avenue. Rock-N-Stroll is made possible through the support of Crossroads, 1st United Credit Union, Kelly S. Wright State Farm Insurance, Page 11 Events, SLATE Contemporary Gallery, Rockridge Voice, Becker Boards, Oaklandside and BART. For the complete entertainment schedule, participating businesses and event information, visit RockridgeDistrict.com.

articles.text: On Monday, August 3, the Piedmont Recreation Department’s First Mondays Reading Group had a strong turnout of 26 participants inside the Piedmont Community Hall for their monthly book discussion. They were there to talk about their August book, The Art Thief by Michael Finkel. This non-fiction tells the true story of Stéphane Breitwieser, history’s most prolific art thief. For over six years, he stole nearly 240 artworks worth up to $2 billion from European museums. He stole these objects during broad daylight from small museums, castles, and churches. Unusually, he never sold any pieces; instead, he kept them in his room in his mother’s attic to admire. His girlfriend, Anne-Catherine Kleinklaus, was his accomplice and acted as his lookout during many of the robberies. They amassed roughly 239 items over 172 separate visits before being caught in 2001. Breitwieser was motivated entirely by an insatiable desire to live surrounded by pure beauty rather than to have wealth. He lived with his girlfriend in his dark, private room, where he felt like a king among priceless artifacts. He was finally caught after returning to a museum for what was supposedly his last theft. His capture led to a shocking conclusion when his mother panicked and destroyed or discarded many of the masterpieces. It’s not often that a reader thinks a non-fiction book is fiction. However, the story of Stéphane Breitwieser and The Art Thief is so amazing that initially that’s what one reader thought. Members of the group generally found the book to be fascinating. The chapters are short, and the book is an enjoyable, easy, fast, good summer read. Readers also found it to be a well-written book. Almost all readers gave it a thumbs up. However, liking the book didn’t mean readers liked the characters. The group thought this was a little unusual. In fact, there wasn’t a character in the book that they liked. Breitwieser was at the top of the list. He was selfish, obsessed, and even a psychopath. He rationalized his criminal behavior and was unable to control his obsessions and actions that harmed others. Breitwieser’s early family life, with a missing father who removed his beautiful works of art from Breitwieser’s life and a mother who seemed to care for nothing other than her son, damaged him. His grandparents were also party to it. There were no guardrails on Breitwieser. His family created a void in his moral character that enabled him to justify stealing anything that appealed to him. The readers thought Breitwieser’s mother was particularly contemptible because her attempt to hide Breitwieser’s crimes destroyed many of the stolen pieces. Breitwieser appreciated the beauty of what he stole. She didn’t. The readers thought she might have been protecting herself too because she must have had an idea that something her son was doing wasn’t right. Breitwieser’s behavior was also abetted by his girlfriend. She became his partner in crime and was a disappointing character in the story too. The group’s discussion expanded into other types of art theft, particularly larger ones. Colonial empires’ looting of less developed countries’ cultural and historical treasures was recognized, as was the unwillingness of their national museums to return the thousands of stolen objects they hold. Readers recognized that art is history and is culturally and even spiritually important for countries. These are crimes too. While most of the readers liked the book, not everyone did. For one, Breitwieser was a “parasite.” Other members of the group found him intolerable. Additionally, the author’s chronicling of his thefts was repetitive and not enjoyable. They would have also liked more information about the psychology behind this type of behavior. However, the readers seemed to agree that The Art Thief was a good book for the First Mondays Reading Group. It was one that most members would not have read, but it generated a stimulating discussion. It also raised important historical, cultural, and societal issues for us to think about. The group had previously selected Horse by Geraldine Brooks for September and Freezing Order by Bill Browder for October. After Phyllis Van Kranenburgh presented three fiction candidates, the readers selected The Correspondent by Virginia Evans for their November read. Arrested Development ran three seasons on Fox before cancellation in 2006, then returned on Netflix for a fourth season in 2013 and a fifth in 2018–2019. The redesigned area will feature state-of-the-art materials for enhanced durability and safety, including new safety matting to replace the existing sand, upgraded ADA access and a refined perimeter for the swing area. To build on this momentum, the PBF Spring Campaign is now focused on creating a nature play area adjacent to the swings.
